description: A soft, succulent little annual whose upper leaves are fused right round the stem into a round green disc, with a short spray of tiny white flowers rising from its centre; long-stalked basal leaves sprawl beneath it, 5-30 cm tall. It carpets the moist, shaded ground under the oaks, along the creeks and on the north slopes from February into May, a fresh green that deer, rabbits, voles and quail all eat, and its shiny black seeds are carried off by ants.

season_notes.winter: Bright green rosettes of long-stalked leaves in the shade of the oaks, thickening after each storm.
season_notes.spring: The round cup-leaves open, each with tiny white flowers at its centre, February into May.
season_notes.summer: Wilted and gone as the shade dries out in June.
season_notes.fall: Nothing above ground until the rains; the seed waits in the leaf litter.

riparian.water: Wants winter-wet, shaded soil: the terraces under the creekside trees, where it grows through the rainy months only.

notes: Miner's lettuce is a cool-season annual of shade and moisture: under oak and bay canopies, in riparian strips, at the foot of north slopes and around seeps, rarely in the open grassland. The basal leaves are long-stalked and spoon- to kidney-shaped; the one pair of stem leaves below the flowers is joined into a single round, cupped disc 1-6 cm across that the stem pierces (leaf shape round, 5 cm, a juicy mid-green); the flowers are 5-petalled, white to faintly pink, about 5 mm, a dozen or so in a short cluster on the disc. It is succulent and mild, which is why so many animals eat it (deer, brush rabbits, voles, ground squirrels; quail take the greens and the seed), and the gold-rush miners ate it as a salad green, which gave the name. Each glossy black seed carries a small fatty appendage that ants harvest, so it is ant-sown. height_by_month: it germinates with the November rains, is fullest in March-April, and wilts in the first dry heat, so it is zero from June through October and its dead_rgb is never really shown. habitat: shade 0.8, north x1.6, the floors and swales x1.4; on dry steep ground and in the sun it is scarce.
